title: II. For A Moment The Lie Becomes Truth
paragraphs: He hurried off to the hospital where Mitya now lay. The day after his fate was decided, Mitya had come down with nervous fever and been sent to the prison ward of the town hospital. But at the request of several people (Alyosha, Madame Hohlakov, Lise, and others), Doctor Varvinsky had placed Mitya not among the other prisoners, but in a small separate room — the same one where Smerdyakov had once stayed. True, there was a sentry posted at the far end of the corridor, and a grating over the window, so Varvinsky could feel reasonably at ease about the leniency he'd shown, even though it wasn't strictly legal; but he was a kindhearted, compassionate young man. He understood how hard it would be for a man like Mitya to be thrown straight into the company of robbers and murderers, and that he needed time to adjust gradually. Visits from relatives and friends were informally allowed by the doctor and the overseer, even by the police captain. But only Alyosha and Grushenka had actually come to see Mitya. Rakitin had tried twice to force his way in, but Mitya kept begging Varvinsky not to let him.

Alyosha found him sitting on his bed in a hospital dressing gown, somewhat feverish, a towel soaked in vinegar and water wrapped around his head. He looked at Alyosha as he came in with an unreadable expression, though something like dread was visible in it. He'd grown terribly preoccupied since the trial; sometimes he'd fall silent for half an hour at a stretch, seeming to brood heavily and painfully over something, oblivious to everything around him. When he roused himself and started talking, he always spoke abruptly, and never about what was really on his mind. Sometimes he looked at his brother with a face full of suffering. He seemed more at ease with Grushenka than with Alyosha. True, he barely spoke to her at all, but the moment she walked in, his whole face lit up with joy.

Alyosha sat down beside him on the bed without a word. This time Mitya was waiting for him in suspense, but didn't dare come out and ask. He felt it was almost unthinkable that Katya would agree to come, and at the same time felt that if she didn't, something unimaginable would happen. Alyosha understood exactly what he was feeling.

“Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began nervously, “has torn his whole inn apart, I hear. Pulled up the flooring, ripped apart the planks, taken the whole gallery to pieces — so they tell me. He's hunting for treasure the whole time — that fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said I'd hidden there. Started playing these games the moment he got home, apparently. Serves him right, the swindler! The guard here told me yesterday — he's from those parts.”
“Listen,” Alyosha began. “She'll come — but I don't know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can't say. But she'll come — she will, that's certain.”

Mitya started; he seemed about to say something, but stayed silent. The news had a tremendous effect on him. It was obvious he was desperate to know exactly what had been said, but he was afraid to ask again. Anything cruel or contemptuous from Katya would have cut him like a knife at that moment.
“Among other things, she said this — that I should make sure to set your conscience at rest about the escape. If Ivan isn't well by then, she'll see to everything herself.”
“You've told me that already,” Mitya said thoughtfully.
“And you've told Grusha, too,” Alyosha observed.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “She won't come this morning.” He looked timidly at his brother. “She won't come until evening. When I told her yesterday that Katya was taking steps, she went quiet — but her mouth set. She only whispered, ‘Let her!’ She understood it mattered. I didn't dare push her any further. I think she understands now that Katya doesn't care for me anymore — that she loves Ivan.”
“Does she?” broke from Alyosha.

“Maybe she doesn't. But she's not coming this morning, that's for sure,” Mitya hurried to explain again. “I asked her to do something for me. You know, Ivan is better than all the rest of us. He ought to live — not us. He'll get well.”
“Would you believe it — though Katya's frightened for him, she hardly doubts he'll recover,” said Alyosha.
“That means she's convinced he'll die. It's exactly because she's so frightened that she's certain he'll get well.”
“Ivan has a strong constitution, and I believe too that there's every hope he'll recover,” Alyosha said, with some anxiety.
“Yes, he'll get well. But she's convinced he'll die. She's got a great deal of grief ahead of her....” A silence followed. Some heavy worry was gnawing at Mitya.
“Alyosha, I love Grusha terribly,” he said suddenly, in a shaking, tearful voice.
“They won't let her come out there with you,” Alyosha put in at once.

“And there's something else I wanted to tell you,” Mitya went on, a new edge suddenly in his voice. “If they beat me on the way there, or once I'm there, I won't stand for it. I'll kill someone, and I'll be shot for it. And this is supposed to go on for twenty years! They already talk to me rudely as it is. I've been lying here all night, sitting in judgment on myself. I'm not ready! I can't resign myself to it. I wanted to sing a ‘hymn’ — but if a guard so much as speaks rudely to me, I don't have the strength to bear it. For Grusha's sake I could bear anything... anything except being beaten.... But they won't even let her come there.”
Alyosha smiled gently.

“Listen, brother, once and for all,” he said. “This is what I think about it. And you know I wouldn't lie to you. Listen: you're not ready, and that kind of cross isn't meant for you. What's more, you don't need a martyr's cross like that when you're not ready for it. If you had murdered our father, it would grieve me to see you refuse your punishment. But you're innocent, and that cross is too heavy for you. You wanted to make yourself into a new man through suffering — I say, just remember that other man, always, your whole life, wherever you go, and that will be enough for you. Refusing that great cross will only leave you with an even deeper sense of duty for the rest of your life, and that constant feeling will do more, perhaps, to remake you than actually going through with it. Because out there, you wouldn't be able to bear it — you'd resent it, and in the end you might well say, ‘I owe them nothing now.’ The lawyer was right about that. Burdens as heavy as that aren't for everyone. For some men they're simply impossible. That's what I think, if you really want to know. If other men would have to answer for your escape — officers, soldiers — then I wouldn't ‘allow’ it,” Alyosha smiled. “But they say — the superintendent at that stopping point told Ivan himself — that if it's handled properly there won't be much of an inquiry, and they can get away with it easily. Of course, bribery is dishonest even in a case like this, but I can't undertake to judge that, because if Ivan and Katya asked me to act for you, I know I'd go and pay the bribes myself. I have to tell you the truth. And so I can't sit in judgment on your own decision. But let me assure you — I will never condemn you for it. And it would be strange indeed if I could judge you on this. Now I think I've covered everything.”

“But I condemn myself!” Mitya cried. “I'll escape — that much was decided without you; could Mitya Karamazov do anything else but run? But I'll condemn myself for it, and I'll pray for my sin forever. That's how the Jesuits talk, isn't it? Just like we're doing now?”
“Yes.” Alyosha smiled gently.

“I love you because you always tell the whole truth and never hide a thing,” Mitya cried, with a joyful laugh. “So I've caught my own Alyosha being a Jesuit. I have to kiss you for that. Now listen to the rest — I'll open up the other side of my heart to you. Here's what I've planned, what I've decided. If I escape — even with money and papers, even to America — I'll be cheered by the thought that I'm not running off for pleasure, not for happiness, but into another kind of exile, maybe just as bad as Siberia. It is just as bad, Alyosha, it is! I already hate that America, damn it. Even with Grusha at my side. Just look at her — is she some American? She's Russian, Russian to the marrow of her bones — she'll be homesick for the motherland, and I'll see it every single hour, that she's suffering for my sake, that she's taken up that cross for me. And what has she ever done wrong? And how am I supposed to put up with the rabble out there, even if every one of them turns out to be better than I am? I already hate that America! And even if they're wonders at machinery, the lot of them, damn them, they're not kindred souls of mine. I love Russia, Alyosha, I love the Russian God, even though I'm a scoundrel myself. I'll choke out there!” he exclaimed, his eyes suddenly blazing. His voice shook with tears. “So here's what I've decided, Alyosha, listen,” he began again, getting his emotion under control. “The moment we arrive there with Grusha, we'll go straight to work on the land, somewhere remote, in solitude, among the wild bears. There must be some remote corner even out there. I'm told there are still Redskins somewhere, way out on the edge of the horizon. So — off to the land of the Last of the Mohicans, and there Grusha and I will tackle the grammar right away. Work and grammar — that's how we'll spend three years. And by the end of it we'll speak English like a couple of Englishmen. And the moment we've learned it — goodbye, America! We'll come running back here to Russia, as American citizens. Don't worry — we won't come to this little town. We'll hide somewhere far off, north or south. I'll be a different man by then, and so will she, over there in America. The doctors will fix me up with some kind of wart on my face — what's the use of them being so mechanical otherwise! — or else I'll put out one eye, grow my beard a yard long, and turn gray pining for Russia. I dare say they won't even recognize us. And if they do, let them send us to Siberia — I don't care. It'll only mean that was our fate. We'll work the land here too, somewhere out in the wilds, and I'll play the American my whole life long. But we'll die on our own soil. That's my plan, and it's final. Do you approve?”
“Yes,” said Alyosha, not wanting to argue with him. Mitya paused for a moment, then said suddenly:
“And how they built it all up at the trial! Didn't they just build it up!”
“If they hadn't, you'd have been convicted just the same,” Alyosha said, with a sigh.
“Yes — people here are sick of the sight of me! God bless them, but it's hard,” Mitya moaned miserably. Again there was a moment of silence.
“Alyosha, put me out of my misery right now!” he burst out suddenly. “Tell me — is she coming now, or isn't she? Tell me! What did she say? How did she say it?”
“She said she'd come, but I don't know if it'll be today. It's hard for her, you know,” Alyosha said, glancing timidly at his brother.

“I should think it's hard for her! Alyosha, it'll drive me out of my mind. Grusha keeps watching me. She understands. My God, calm my heart down — what is it I even want? I want Katya! Do I even understand what I want? It's this headstrong, wicked Karamazov spirit! No — I'm not fit for suffering. I'm a scoundrel, that's all there is to say.”
“Here she is!” Alyosha cried.

At that instant Katya appeared in the doorway. For a moment she stood frozen, staring at Mitya with a dazed expression. He sprang impulsively to his feet, and a frightened look crossed his face. He went pale, but a timid, pleading smile appeared on his lips at once, and with an irresistible impulse he stretched out both hands to Katya. Seeing this, she rushed toward him. She seized his hands and, almost by force, made him sit down on the bed. She sat beside him, still gripping his hands, pressing them hard. Several times they both tried to speak, but stopped short and simply stared at each other in silence, a strange smile on both their faces, their eyes locked. Two minutes passed like this.
“Have you forgiven me?” Mitya finally faltered, and at the same instant, turning to Alyosha, his face working with joy, cried, “Do you hear what I'm asking, do you hear?”

“That's exactly what I loved you for — that generous heart of yours!” burst from Katya. “My forgiveness is no use to you, and yours is no use to me. Whether you forgive me or not, you'll always be a sore spot in my heart, and I in yours — that's simply how it has to be....” She stopped to catch her breath. “What did I come here for?” she began again, with nervous haste. “To embrace your feet, to press your hands like this, until it hurts — remember how I used to squeeze them in Moscow? — to tell you again that you're my god, my joy, to tell you that I love you madly,” she moaned in anguish, and suddenly pressed his hand greedily to her lips. Tears streamed from her eyes. Alyosha stood speechless, dumbfounded — he had never expected what he was seeing now.

“Love is over, Mitya!” Katya began again. “But the past is painfully dear to me. Know that it will always be that way. But now — for just one minute — let what might have been come true,” she faltered, a strained smile on her face, gazing at him again with a kind of joy. “You love another woman, and I love another man, and yet I will love you forever, and you'll love me — do you know that? Do you hear me? Love me — love me your whole life!” she cried, a quiver almost like a threat in her voice.

“I will love you, and... do you know, Katya,” Mitya began, drawing a deep breath between each word, “do you know, five days ago — that very evening — I loved you.... When you fell and they carried you out... All my life! So it will be, so it will always be—”
So they murmured frantic words to one another, almost meaningless, maybe not even true, but at that moment it was all true, and they both believed every word of it without question.
“Katya,” Mitya cried suddenly, “do you believe I murdered him? I know you don't believe it now — but back then... when you gave your testimony.... Surely, surely you didn't believe it!”

“I didn't believe it even then. I've never believed it. I hated you, and for a moment I talked myself into it. While I was giving my testimony I convinced myself, and believed it — but the moment I finished speaking I stopped believing it at once. Don't doubt that! I'd forgotten I came here to punish myself,” she said, a new note in her voice now, utterly unlike the loving tone of a moment before.
“Woman, yours is a heavy burden to bear,” broke, almost involuntarily, from Mitya.
“Let me go,” she whispered. “I'll come again. It's more than I can bear right now.”

She was rising to leave, but suddenly let out a loud scream and staggered back. Grushenka had come into the room, suddenly and without a sound. No one had expected her. Katya moved swiftly toward the door, but when she reached Grushenka she stopped short, turned white as chalk, and murmured, almost in a whisper:
“Forgive me!”
Grushenka stared at her, and after a moment's pause, answered in a vindictive, venomous voice:
“We're both full of hatred, my girl — you and I! Both of us, full of hatred! As if we could ever forgive each other! Save him, and I'll worship you for the rest of my life.”
“You won't forgive her!” Mitya cried, in frantic reproach.
“Don't worry — I'll save him for you!” Katya whispered rapidly, and ran out of the room.
“And you could refuse to forgive her, when she herself begged your forgiveness?” Mitya exclaimed bitterly again.
“Mitya, don't you dare blame her — you have no right to!” Alyosha cried hotly.
“Her proud lips were talking, not her heart,” Grushenka said, in a tone of disgust. “If she saves you, I'll forgive her everything—”
She fell silent, as though holding something back. She still hadn't recovered herself. She'd come in, as it turned out afterward, purely by chance, with no idea what she'd find.
“Alyosha, run after her!” Mitya cried to his brother. “Tell her... I don't know... don't let her leave like this!”
“I'll come back to see you tonight,” Alyosha said, and ran after Katya. He caught up with her outside the hospital grounds. She was walking fast, but the moment Alyosha reached her, she said quickly:

“No — in front of that woman, I can't punish myself! I asked for her forgiveness because I wanted to punish myself to the very end. She wouldn't forgive me.... I like her for that!” she added, in a strained voice, her eyes flashing with fierce resentment.
“My brother didn't expect this in the least,” Alyosha muttered. “He was sure she wouldn't come—”

“No doubt. Let's leave that alone,” she snapped. “Listen: I can't go with you to the funeral now. I've already sent them flowers. I believe they still have some money. If it's needed, tell them I'll never abandon them.... Now leave me — please, leave me. You're already late as it is — the bells are ringing for the service.... Leave me, please!”
